what: Step 2 — Choose an objective environmental resolution
title: Day 2 — Environmental thinning with bean
text: find_env_resolution() derives per-variable environmental grid resolution kernel-density bandwidth variable’s marginal distribution. intuition: bandwidth scale, two occurrences carry essentially environmental information, natural cell width thinning. function returns one suggested resolution per environmental variable, units variable. Three classic bandwidth selectors supported: "sheather-jones" (default) — Sheather & Jones (1991) plug-selector; robust non-Gaussian data modern recommended default. "silverman" — Silverman’s rule thumb; fast stable distribution roughly Gaussian. "scott" — Scott’s rule; Gaussian-optimal variant Silverman. Sheather–Jones fails (can happen strongly tied data) function automatically falls back Silverman’s rule variable emits message.  comparison, try Silverman’s rule thumb — usually returns slightly larger (smoother) cell width assumes near-Gaussian shape:
code: res_search <- find_env_resolution(data = prepped,                                   env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                   method = "sheather-jones")  # The print method shows one row per variable res_search ## --- Bean environmental grid resolution --- ## Bandwidth selector: sheather-jones ##  ##  variable  resolution ##      bio1 0.055443572 ##     bio12 0.004124131 ##     bio15 0.005982760 # The plot method draws one KDE panel per variable, with the bandwidth # shown as a red scale bar = the suggested cell width plot(res_search) # The named numeric vector we'll pass to the thinning functions below chosen_res <- res_search$suggested_resolution chosen_res ##        bio1       bio12       bio15  ## 0.055443572 0.004124131 0.005982760 res_silverman <- find_env_resolution(data = prepped,                                      env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                      method = "silverman") res_silverman ## --- Bean environmental grid resolution --- ## Bandwidth selector: silverman ##  ##  variable resolution ##      bio1 0.17774967 ##     bio12 0.01304209 ##     bio15 0.02203666

text: Now download every available occurrence record Sambar deer (Rusa unicolor) Thailand GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility) — largest open database species records world. GBIF records carry basisOfRecord tag tells record generated. ecological niche modelling want records represent contemporary, free-living distribution species, keep field observations: HUMAN_OBSERVATION — person directly observed animal field (e.g. wildlife survey citizen-science sighting). gold standard ENM. OBSERVATION — generic observation record, less specific HUMAN_OBSERVATION. Still field record, keep . OCCURRENCE — catch-“species time” record. include excluding discard otherwise usable field data. exclude categories represent contemporary, wild, -situ animals: FOSSIL_SPECIMEN — animal lived long ago; relevant today’s climate niche. PRESERVED_SPECIMEN — museum herbarium material; locality information often skewed toward roads, towns, historical expeditions. LIVING_SPECIMEN — captive animals zoos breeding centres; location says nothing wild niche. MATERIAL_SAMPLE / MACHINE_OBSERVATION — DNA samples automated detections (e.g. camera traps, acoustic loggers). valuable require dedicated processing pipelines excluded simplicity. work GBIF pipeline five short sub-steps .

code: allowed_basis <- c("HUMAN_OBSERVATION", "OCCURRENCE", "OBSERVATION")  # Query GBIF once per basisOfRecord category. `lapply()` returns a list of # data frames, one per category, which we then row-bind into a single table. raw_list <- lapply(allowed_basis, function(b) {   rgbif::occ_search(     taxonKey           = key,         # unique taxon identifier from Sub-step 2     country            = "TH",        # ISO-2 country code for Thailand     basisOfRecord      = b,           # this category only     hasCoordinate      = TRUE,        # drop records without lon/lat     hasGeospatialIssue = FALSE,       # drop records with known coord problems     limit              = 5000         # generous upper bound per category   )$data })  raw <- dplyr::bind_rows(raw_list)  # Belt-and-braces: re-apply the basisOfRecord filter on the combined table # in case the API quietly returns something we did not ask for. raw <- raw %>% filter(basisOfRecord %in% allowed_basis)  # Save the raw download to disk so we have a snapshot we can re-read later # without re-hitting GBIF. write_csv(raw, file.path(gbif_dir, "sambar_gbif.csv"))  nrow(raw)

code: # Re-read the raw snapshot we just wrote. sambar <- read_csv(file.path(gbif_dir, "sambar_gbif.csv"))  # Keep only the columns we will need downstream and drop rows with missing # coordinates (we already asked GBIF for `hasCoordinate = TRUE`, but a final # sanity check is cheap). sambar <- raw %>%   select(species,          decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude,          year, month,          basisOfRecord, gbifID) %>%   filter(!is.na(decimalLongitude),          !is.na(decimalLatitude),          basisOfRecord %in% allowed_basis)  # Turn the table into spatial points (CRS 4326 = WGS84 longitude/latitude). # `remove = FALSE` keeps the numeric lon/lat columns alongside the geometry. sambar_sf <- st_as_sf(sambar,                       coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),                       crs    = 4326,                       remove = FALSE)  # Test which records actually fall inside the Thailand polygon. `st_within()` # returns a one-column logical matrix, so we pull out column 1. inside  <- st_within(sambar_sf, tha_sf, sparse = FALSE)[, 1] sambar  <- sambar[inside, ]

text: nicheR ellipsoid built range data frame lists lowest highest value species tolerates along environmental axis. ranges, build_ellipsoid() derives every geometric property niche: centroid (midpoint ranges), covariance matrix (axes co-vary), semi-axis lengths (half-width ellipsoid direction), niche volume. virtual tropical mammal set: bio1 (mean annual T) 25 °C 28 °C — warm, narrow thermal niche. bio12 (annual precip.) 1200 mm 2500 mm — wet extreme. bio15 (precip. seasonality, CV) 70 90 — moderately strongly seasonal rainfall. Together three windows describe small, well-defined ellipsoid sitting lowland, seasonally-wet corner Thailand’s environmental space. Printing ell shows compact summary niche. Reading output line line: Dimensions: 3D. Three environmental axes, ellipsoid true 3-D shape (“egg” BIO1 × BIO12 × BIO15 space). Chi-square cutoff: 11.345. 95% probability boundary niche, taken chi-square distribution 3 degrees freedom. Pixels squared Mahalanobis distance cutoff fall inside niche; rest outside. Centroid (mu): (26.5, 1850, 80). geometric centre ranges — preferred environmental conditions. Covariance matrix. diagonal matrix three ranges specified independently — axis varies cross-axis covariances zero. Ellipsoid semi-axis lengths: 729.78, 11.227, 1.684. half-widths ellipsoid direction. Notice stretched bio12 axis (precipitation values span hundreds mm) compared bio15 (CV values span tens) — ellipsoid elongated along precipitation. Ellipsoid axis endpoints. two vertex coordinates ends axis — useful sanity-checking ellipsoid actually reaches ranges specified. Ellipsoid volume: 57 800.1. total amount E-space niche occupies, mixed units. Useful comparing niche breadths species. can visualise ellipsoid E-space cloud environmental conditions Thailand actually offers — background point cloud. Every grey dot one pixel country plotted BIO1 × BIO12 (third axis, BIO15, collapsed 2-D view). niche sits inside cloud can realised geographically; niche sits outside cloud produce empty suitability map.  ellipse plot 2-D projection niche onto BIO1 × BIO12 plane. grey dots background point cloud. Pixels fall inside ellipse correspond places map virtual species can occur; pixels outside ellipse environmentally unsuitable.

what: Project the niche to geography (suitability + Mahalanobis distance)
title: Step 1 — Virtual species with nicheR
text: predict() projects ellipsoid E-space onto SpatRaster environmental conditions (, Thailand env_space stack) returns two surfaces, layer layer: Suitability. 0–1 score peaks 1 centroid falls smoothly toward boundary. suitability_truncated = TRUE, pixels outside niche clamped 0, giving cleaner “” answer layer called suitability_trunc. Mahalanobis distance. multivariate distance centroid takes shape correlations niche account. Low = environmentally similar centre niche; high = far . truncated version (Mahal_trunc) also produced. short, suitability probability-like score plot map, Mahalanobis distance raw geometric distance used compute . printout describes pred SpatRaster 89 × 50 pixels 7 layers. min values / max values rows give range layer across pixels.
code: pred <- predict(   ell,                                # the ellipsoid we just built   newdata               = env_space,  # SpatRaster to project onto   include_suitability   = TRUE,       # return the suitability surface   suitability_truncated = TRUE,       # also return a clamped (in/out) version   include_mahalanobis   = TRUE,       # return the Mahalanobis-distance surface   mahalanobis_truncated = TRUE,       # also return a clamped version   keep_data             = TRUE        # keep the original env layers in `pred` )  # pred is now a multi-layer SpatRaster carrying: the three predictors # (bio1, bio12, bio15), the two suitability layers (full + truncated), and # the two Mahalanobis layers (full + truncated). pred ## class       : SpatRaster  ## size        : 89, 50, 7  (nrow, ncol, nlyr) ## resolution  : 0.1666667, 0.1666667  (x, y) ## extent      : 97.33333, 105.6667, 5.666667, 20.5  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) ## coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)  ## sources     : bioclim_thailand.tif  (3 layers)  ##               memory   ##               memory   ##               ... and 2 more sources ## names       :     bio1, bio12,     bio15, Mahalanobis,  suitability, Mahal~trunc, ...  ## min values  : 20.52728,   806,  37.47298,   0.8032656, 5.926184e-43,   0.8032656, ...  ## max values  : 28.89861,  4101, 109.94184, 194.4635571, 6.692265e-01,  11.2917557, ... plot(pred, col = viridis::viridis(100)) # A "binary potential distribution" is just the truncated suitability # turned into 1 / 0: 1 wherever the niche is realised, 0 elsewhere. binary_rast <- (pred$suitability_trunc > 0) * 1  plot(binary_rast,      axes = FALSE,                              # hide longitude/latitude tick labels      box  = TRUE,                               # keep the surrounding frame      col  = c("#d4d4d4", "#0004d5"),            # grey = unsuitable, blue = suitable      main = "Potential Distribution (Binary)")

Many recorded species pixel implies many surveys done . treat richness direct proxy: higher richness → sampling effort. Night-time lights — satellite measure artificial light. High light values mark cities roads. remote Sambar deer habitat dark, treat night-time lights inverse proxy: light → less relevant sampling effort forest-dwelling virtual species.   multiply suitability bias surface get realised sampling probability. Pixels suitable species easy survey light ; pixels biologically suitable remote areas dim .  biological niche identical maps, realised-sampling surface concentrates around accessible, biodiversity-rich pixels Thailand — parts niche realistically generate records biased field survey.
code: sp_rich_layer   <- rast("data/processed/bias/sp_richness_TH.tif") nighttime_layer <- rast("data/processed/bias/nighttime_TH.tif")  # Stack the two proxies into a 2-layer SpatRaster and rename for clarity. bias_layer <- c(sp_rich_layer, nighttime_layer) names(bias_layer) <- c("sp_richness", "nighttime_light") plot(bias_layer) # prepare_bias() rescales each proxy to 0-1, optionally inverts proxies whose # *high* values represent *low* sampling effort, and combines the two into a # single composite surface. `effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse")` # tells it to use richness directly but invert night-time lights. bias_prep <- prepare_bias(   bias_surface     = bias_layer,   effect_direction = c("direct", "inverse") )  # The composite surface is a 0-1 map of "how likely a survey would happen # here": high values mark accessible, biodiversity-rich pixels; low values # mark remote, brightly-lit-but-empty pixels (essentially, urban areas). plot(bias_prep$composite_surface) biased_pred <- apply_bias(   prepared_bias    = bias_prep,                 # the composite bias surface from prepare_bias()   prediction       = pred,                      # the projected ellipsoid from predict()   prediction_layer = "suitability",             # which layer of `pred` to multiply against bias   effect_direction = "direct"                   # high bias → high realised sampling )  par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(pred$suitability,      main = "Unbiased suitability") plot(biased_pred$suitability_biased,      main = "Suitability × bias = realised sampling surface") par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

text: find_env_resolution() derives grid resolution thinning directly data. per variable, meaning returns one suggested cell width environmental axis (BIO1 gets width, BIO12 gets different width, BIO15 gets yet another), natural units variable. widths come kernel-density bandwidth variable’s marginal distribution: bandwidth scale, two occurrences carry essentially environmental information, natural cell width extra records redundant. Three classic bandwidth selectors supported: "sheather-jones" (default) — Sheather & Jones (1991) plug-selector; robust non-Gaussian shapes modern recommended default. "silverman" — Silverman’s rule thumb; fast stable distribution roughly Gaussian. "scott" — Scott’s rule; Gaussian-optimal variant Silverman. Sheather–Jones fails (can happen strongly tied data) function automatically falls back Silverman’s rule variable emits message. run three selectors compare , pick one feed thinning step. Read across row compare. Silverman Scott simple plug-ins assume roughly Gaussian distribution, usually return similar, slightly larger bandwidths, coarser cells, fewer pods, aggressive thinning. Sheather–Jones data-adaptive usually smaller, finer cells, pods, gentler thinning. real occurrence data, almost never Gaussian, recommend "sheather-jones": preserves environmental nuance safest default workshop. method’s diagnostic plot. panel kernel-density estimate (KDE) one bioclim variable; red horizontal scale bar marks bandwidth selector chose — .e. suggested cell width.    Reading panels: black curve kernel-density estimate occurrence points distributed along environmental axis; shaded area curve helps eye see bulk density sits; red horizontal bar suggested cell width (= bandwidth) centred mode density. narrower bar means finer grid gentler thinning; wider bar means coarser grid aggressive thinning. use Sheather–Jones rest analysis:
code: res_sj       <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "sheather-jones") res_silverman <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "silverman") res_scott    <- find_env_resolution(prepped,                                     env_vars = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),                                     method   = "scott")  # Side-by-side comparison: one column per selector, one row per variable, # values in z-score units (we scaled the data in prepare_bean()). cbind(   sheather_jones = res_sj$suggested_resolution,   silverman      = res_silverman$suggested_resolution,   scott          = res_scott$suggested_resolution ) ##       sheather_jones  silverman      scott ## bio1     0.055443572 0.17774967 0.20934961 ## bio12    0.004124131 0.01304209 0.01536068 ## bio15    0.005982760 0.02203666 0.02595429 plot(res_sj) plot(res_silverman) plot(res_scott) chosen_res <- res_sj$suggested_resolution chosen_res ##        bio1       bio12       bio15  ## 0.055443572 0.004124131 0.005982760

title: Step 2 — Environmental thinning with bean
text: bean ships two thinning strategies: thin_env_nd() — stochastic. Builds grid, finds every occupied pod, randomly retains one original occurrences pod. Real coordinates GBIF metadata preserved. thin_env_center() — deterministic. Builds grid replaces points occupied pod single synthetic point centre pod. Output reproducible without seed, points longer real observations. run comparison.   Reading plots: pale grey dots original occurrences (cloud saw E-space panel earlier); highlighted markers points survive thinning. thin_env_nd highlighted markers sit top original cloud (real points kept); thin_env_center sit regular grid points centres occupied pods (synthetic locations). Notice methods break dense cluster dominated raw E-space plot.
code: # Stochastic thinning: one randomly chosen occurrence per pod. thin_nd <- thin_env_nd(   data            = prepped,   env_vars        = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),   grid_resolution = chosen_res          # per-variable cell widths from Sheather-Jones )  # Deterministic thinning: one synthetic point at the centre of each pod. # We deliberately use a fixed, coarse resolution here (0.5 z-score units on # every axis). Because the data were scaled in prepare_bean(), 0.5 means # half a standard deviation per axis — a sensible "moderate smoothing" # choice that is easy to interpret and visualise. thin_center <- thin_env_center(   data            = prepped,   env_vars        = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15"),   grid_resolution = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) )  # Each `thin_*` object reports the number of input occurrences, the number # of occupied pods, the retained sample size, and stores the thinned table # in `$thinned_data`. thin_nd ## --- Bean Stochastic Thinning Results --- ##  ## Thinned 1031 original points to 80 points. ## This represents a retention of 7.8% of the data. ##  ## -------------------------------------- thin_center ## --- Bean Deterministic Thinning Results --- ##  ## Thinned 1031 original points to 42 unique grid cell centers. ## This represents a retention of 4.1% of the data. ##  ## -------------------------------------- # `plot_bean()` overlays the original data (grey, faded) and the retained # thinned points (highlighted) on the same E-space scatter. plot_bean(   original_data  = prepped,   thinned_object = thin_nd,   env_vars       = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15") ) plot_bean(   original_data  = prepped,   thinned_object = thin_center,   env_vars       = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15") )

text: thinning, build single temporal-mean reference E-space summarises environment Sambar deer experienced across entire 2010–2025 window. compute per-pixel mean across years three aligned variables, stack three mean surfaces one 3-layer SpatRaster. temporal-mean stack reference environmental space bean uses thin every year. Using single, period-wide E-space (rather year-specific raster occurrence) keeps thinning grid consistent across years: 2014 record 2020 record fall temporal-mean pod treated environmentally redundant, even though individual years’ rasters may differ slightly.  Reading panels: map per-pixel average corresponding variable across 16 modelled years, variable’s natural units (mm precipitation, °C-equivalent units land-surface-temperature-derived temp, unitless 0–1 index NDVI). Bright patches stand places consistently wet, warm, vegetated; dark patches stand places consistently dry, cool, sparse. environmental landscape bean use define thinning grid.
code: # List every aligned per-year raster, then split by variable name. aligned_files <- list.files(aligned_dir, pattern = "\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)  # Group the file list by variable name (prec_ / temp_ / NDVI_) so each # group becomes a multi-layer SpatRaster spanning every year. prec_files <- file.path(aligned_dir,                         grep("prec_",  basename(aligned_files), value = TRUE)) temp_files <- file.path(aligned_dir,                         grep("temp_",  basename(aligned_files), value = TRUE)) NDVI_files <- file.path(aligned_dir,                         grep("NDVI_",  basename(aligned_files), value = TRUE))  # Per-pixel mean across years for each variable — terra::mean() over a # multi-layer SpatRaster collapses the time dimension into a single layer. mean_prec <- terra::mean(rast(prec_files), na.rm = TRUE) mean_temp <- terra::mean(rast(temp_files), na.rm = TRUE) mean_NDVI <- terra::mean(rast(NDVI_files), na.rm = TRUE)  # Stack the three mean surfaces into one 3-layer reference E-space, and # rename the layers to the variable names bean will look up. env_ref <- c(mean_prec, mean_temp, mean_NDVI) names(env_ref) <- c("mean_prec", "mean_temp", "mean_NDVI")  par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) plot(mean_prec, main = "Mean precipitation (2010–2025)") plot(mean_temp, main = "Mean temperature (2010–2025)") plot(mean_NDVI, main = "Mean NDVI (2010–2025)") par(mfrow = c(1, 1))     # reset the plot region back to a single panel
